question: Classify, one class per intake: local, cross-node, new-capability or structural?

options.label: cross-node
options.consequence: The existing root and its three leaf-parents take the change: ADR and contract handoffs first, then node touches, then phases appended on backend, web and integration. No node is added and the tree keeps its shape.

options.label: new-capability
options.consequence: A booking node (or a database node) is grafted under simple-login. It splits work one developer owns across two nodes, or gives one developer's database a node of its own, against the root's who-builds-what axis.

options.label: structural
options.consequence: A shape stop: the tree is re-cut (for example by feature: login and booking, each full-stack). The owner answers before anything is planned.

chosen: cross-node
why: The root's decomposition axis is who builds what: the backend developer builds the service, the frontend developer builds the web app, and the integration node runs both. PRD v2 Team and delivery keeps exactly that split and adds that the backend developer owns the database, and the owner's facts repeat it and keep the integration node as the place where both run together. So rooms, bookings and PostgreSQL land in simple-login.backend, the Rooms screen and my bookings in simple-login.web, and the scripted success tests in simple-login.integration: several existing nodes' surfaces, joined through contracts, with no missing node and nothing wrong with the shape. Each leaf-parent still has one owner who can hold its scope and splits into review-sized phases, so none needs to become internal. A third developer, or a booking feature owned by a different team, would have made new-capability or structural the leading option.

question: Which new contract or contracts carry PRD v2 US-4 to US-6 across the backend to web seam?

options.consequence: One file, schema and fixture set for the rooms on a date, booking, my bookings and cancelling. The booking shape is defined once and versions once. A change to the rooms view alone still bumps the whole contract.

options.label: two contracts, room-api@v1 and booking-api@v1
options.consequence: The read view (rooms with their bookings on a date) and the write side (book, my bookings, cancel) version separately, following the auth-api and profile-api split. The booking shape appears in both, so a change to it bumps two contracts in step.

chosen: one contract, booking-api@v1
why: Both options have the same producer (simple-login.backend) and the same consumers (simple-login.web and simple-login.integration). The rooms view of AC-4.2 and AC-4.3, my bookings of AC-6.1 and the conflict message of AC-5.3 all show the same booking (room, title, start, end), so a split would define that shape twice and force lockstep bumps under hsdd-contract's per-version rules. Rooms are pre-loaded and never managed in the app (PRD v2 Rooms, Scope), so they have no lifecycle of their own to version apart. The auth-api and profile-api split does not transfer: those carry disjoint shapes. If rooms were managed in the app, or a consumer read rooms without bookings, the split would lead.

options.consequence: hsdd-contract amends v2 in place under its additive-only rule: timeZone joins the schema as an optional field and the me-ayu and me-budi fixtures carry it. Consumers that ignore unknown fields keep working; no migration window, no deprecation of v2.

options.consequence: A new version with timeZone required, its own schema and fixtures, a migration mode, and profile-api@v2 deprecated or coexisting. Every node naming profile-api@v2 gets a citation move and a migration phase.

why: profile-api@v2 declares compatibility additive-only, and its own Guarantees and Versioning say it may later gain optional fields and that a later optional field keeps v2; hsdd-contract allows that only when the existing fixtures still pass against the changed schema, which an optional field satisfies. The contract's own rule therefore leads. The touch step classifies the change itself; if it finds that consumers must be able to rely on timeZone being present in every profile, which an optional field cannot promise, it classifies the change as breaking and the bump follows from there.
evidence: PRD v2 AC-2.1, AC-2.5, Demo accounts

question: Where is 'whether signing in survives a restart of the service, now that a database exists' (PRD v2 Left to engineering) decided?

options.label: adr-update on ADR-001
options.consequence: hsdd-adr revisits the session model across backend, web and the contracts that take the token: an amendment if the store stays in memory, a superseding ADR if it moves into PostgreSQL. ADR-001's Context, which rests on PRD 1's no database and two endpoints, is brought up to date in the same step.

options.label: backend D{n} in its appended phase plan
options.consequence: The backend decides alone and emits amends; ADR-001 keeps stating that restarting signs everyone out and that there is no database, which PRD v2 makes false, and the web and integration nodes learn of the change only through reconcile.

why: ADR-001 is the accepted decision for the session store, binds backend, web and both token-taking contracts, and lists 'Restarting the backend signs every user out' among its consequences; its Context cites the two-endpoint API and the ruled-out database. Changing or reaffirming the store is therefore ADR-001's to record, per hsdd-adr's ADR or D{n} table. The answer also reaches the integration node: simple-login.integration.2 uses a backend restart as its expired-token stand-in for AC-2.3, which only works while sessions die on restart, so the prompt names it. The same step decides whether sign-out stays client-side now that the endpoint count is no longer fixed.

question: Does the time handling PRD v2 asks for (AC-2.5, AC-4.2 to AC-4.4, AC-5.2, AC-5.3, AC-5.5, AC-6.2) get an ADR, or is it left to the contracts and node-local decisions?

options.label: contracts and D{n} only
options.consequence: booking-api states its wire format; each node decides conversion and formatting locally. The rule that holds the nodes together (which side converts, which clock is authoritative) has no single home and is re-derived by each planner.

chosen: new ADR-002, the time model
why: The decision spans simple-login.backend (storage, the day range, the 'already started' check), simple-login.web (display in the user's zone, the conflict message of AC-5.3), simple-login.integration (London's clock-change days, AC-4.4) and two contracts (profile-api's time zone, booking-api's times). hsdd-adr records a decision that affects more than one node or contract as an ADR. The ADR says why; booking-api and profile-api say what, per hsdd-adr. If only the backend handled time and the web displayed preformatted strings, a D{n} would have sufficed.
evidence: PRD v2 Goal, AC-2.5, AC-4.2 to AC-4.4, AC-5.2, AC-5.3, AC-5.5, AC-6.2

question: Does persistence in PostgreSQL 17 (PRD v2 Constraints) get an ADR of its own?

options.label: no ADR: a root hard constraint plus backend D{n}
options.consequence: The root states PostgreSQL 17 under Docker Compose as a hard constraint from PRD v2; the driver, schema, migrations and the overlap guard behind AC-5.4 are the backend's D{n}; the integration node reaches the database only through the running service, as it reaches the service today.

options.label: ADR-003, persistence
options.consequence: A third ADR records a choice the PRD already made, plus how the database is started for tests and dev; backend and integration cite it. One more binding record to keep current.

chosen: no ADR: a root hard constraint plus backend D{n}
why: PostgreSQL 17 under Docker Compose is a product constraint, not an engineering choice, so it belongs with the root's hard constraints, the way 'no database' did under PRD 1. The owner's facts and PRD v2 Team and delivery give the database to the backend developer, so what is chosen about it (driver, schema, migrations, how exactly-one-wins is enforced) dies with simple-login.backend and is a D{n} by hsdd-adr's table. Which sessions live there is ADR-001's (DEC-008). If a later planner finds the integration node must reach the database directly (to seed or reset bookings) rather than through the service or a backend script, the choice becomes cross-node and an ADR would lead.

options.label: resolve locally, flag upstream
options.consequence: The tree records the new technical approach in ADR-001's update, ADR-002, booking-api@v1, the root's hard constraints and the web's D4; RFC-001 stays as written and the decision is flagged so the developers can amend it or write an RFC for version 2.

options.consequence: The run waits for the developers to write the technical approach for version 2 outside the repository; nothing is planned until then.

Each stale statement already has a home in this record's handoffs: sessions and sign-out in ADR-001's update (DEC-008), times in ADR-002 (DEC-009), the endpoints in booking-api@v1 (DEC-006), the database in the root's constraints (DEC-010), the router in web D4 (DEC-012). question: Which nodes take a spec-touch for a change to their own text (not for contract versions in their headers, which reconcile writes)?

options.label: the root and all three leaf-parents
options.consequence: Four touches: the root's purpose, ownership, hard constraints and decisions; each child's Purpose, Owns, Isolation strategy and Overview, with the root's embedded summary of it. Every node's header says what it now does before its phases are appended.

options.label: the root, backend and web only
options.consequence: Three touches; the integration node's Owns and Isolation strategy keep saying it runs the service and the web app and drives a browser, while its new phases also run PostgreSQL and HTTP-level concurrency and restart tests.

options.label: the root only
options.consequence: One touch; the leaf-parents' headers stay at version 1 scope and their appended phases describe work their Purpose and Owns lines do not cover. Append mode cannot fix those lines.

chosen: the root and all three leaf-parents
why: The root's text is false under PRD v2 (no database, exactly two endpoints, persistence not owned). simple-login.backend's Purpose and Owns lack rooms, bookings and the database, and its Isolation strategy ('no open port needed') must say bookings tests run against a real PostgreSQL (PRD v2 Constraints). simple-login.web's Purpose, Owns and Overview ('Two screens and no router') lack the Rooms screen and my bookings. simple-login.integration's Owns names only a browser test, while PRD v2 Success adds 20 simultaneous booking attempts and a restart that keeps bookings, which it runs against the real service with its database. Append mode never edits a node header's lines other than Sources, so only a touch fixes them. The integration touch is the closest call; had PRD v2 Success been coverable by browser tests alone, it would have been dropped.

question: Whether signing in survives a restart of the service, now that a database exists (PRD v2 Left to engineering): do sessions stay in the backend's in-memory store or move into PostgreSQL?

options.label: sessions stay in memory; amend ADR-001
options.consequence: A restart keeps signing every user out, as today. No shipped code changes, no guarantee of auth-api@v1, profile-api@v1 or profile-api@v2 changes, and simple-login.integration.2's restart stays a valid expired-token stand-in for AC-2.3. ADR-001 is amended in place, not superseded. Users signed in during a restart must sign in again; their bookings are still there.

options.label: sessions move into PostgreSQL; supersede ADR-001
options.consequence: Signing in survives a restart. The backend gains a sessions table and its migration, every token check becomes a database read, and the session tests need the real PostgreSQL. simple-login.integration.2's AC-2.3 stand-in stops working and needs a replacement: a seeded token needs the web app's storage key, which is web-internal (web D2), or the service needs a test-only expiry hook. The H-2 manual check in hsdd/management/2026-10-30-execution-plan.md, which restarts to expire the session, changes too. The superseding ADR takes the next number, ADR-002, which H2 already names for the time model, so one of them is renumbered.

options.label: stateless signed tokens; supersede ADR-001
options.consequence: Signing in survives a restart with no database read, but the token stops being 43 characters of base64url, which auth-api@v1's Interface guarantees: a breaking change to a stable versioned contract, so auth-api@v2 and a migration for every consumer. Adds key management and loses revocation, the reasons RFC-001 §3 rejected it.

chosen: sessions stay in memory; amend ADR-001
why: PRD v2 Left to engineering accepts either answer for the demo, so the choice is engineering cost against a benefit no criterion asks for. PRD v2 Success and Constraints require bookings, not sessions, to survive a restart. Keeping the in-memory store is RFC-001 §3's accepted choice by the two developers, so nothing of theirs is overridden; only its reason changes from 'no database' to PRD v2's 'either is acceptable'. It also keeps the shipped AC-2.3 stand-in in simple-login.integration.2 (a restart gives the same 401 body as an expired token, observed in simple-login.integration.1's verification) and the execution plan's H-2 check. Moving sessions into PostgreSQL would cost a table, a migration, a database read per request and a new expired-token technique for the integration suite, for no stated gain. A PRD criterion that a user stays signed in across a restart, or a deployment with more than one service process (root OQ1), would have made the PostgreSQL option lead.

question: Does sign-out stay client-side now that the API is no longer fixed at two endpoints (RFC-001 §3: 'Revisit if the API grows')?

options.label: client-side, no logout endpoint
options.consequence: Nothing changes in auth-api@v1, the backend or the web app's shipped sign-out; AC-3.1 stays met by the web app discarding its token. A token copied before sign-out keeps working until it expires, at most 30 minutes, and with booking-api@v1 it can now book and cancel in its user's name in that window.

options.label: server-side revocation, a logout endpoint
options.consequence: Sign-out ends the session at once on the server. Costs a new endpoint (an addition to auth-api@v1 or a new contract), a backend task, a change to the web app's shipped sign-out flow (web.3) and an integration test, for no PRD v2 criterion: US-3 is unchanged and Scope does not list it.

chosen: client-side, no logout endpoint
why: RFC-001 §3 made sign-out client-side because PRD 1 fixed the API at two endpoints and asked to revisit if the API grows; booking-api@v1 grows it, so this is that revisit. PRD v2 keeps US-3 with AC-3.1 only, its Scope In does not name sign-out, and it runs on one laptop (PRD v2 Constraints), so the exposure is a token copied from the same laptop's browser within 30 minutes. That exposure now includes booking and cancelling, which the ADR's Consequences state. A deployment beyond the laptop (root OQ1) or a criterion about shared devices would have made the logout endpoint lead.

question: With the decision kept, where does the amendment state what PRD v2 changes for consumers: only in a new ## Amendments section, or also in ## Consequences?

options.label: Amendments only
options.consequence: Decision and Consequences stay byte for byte. hsdd-config injects only those two sections into a phase context, so the booking phases would never see that bookings survive the restart that signs users out, that every endpoint taking the token rejects it the same way, or that a copied token can now book and cancel.

options.label: Consequences amended in place, recorded under Amendments
options.consequence: Decision stays byte for byte; Consequences gain two bullets and two existing bullets gain a clause, all worded without contract or phase ids, so hsdd-config's self-contained rule pulls nothing new into every context ADR-001 governs. The Amendments entries list each change and its reason.

chosen: Consequences amended in place, recorded under Amendments
why: hsdd-adr allows an in-place change that keeps the decision when an Amendments entry records it, and hsdd-config injects Decision and Consequences only, so text a consuming phase needs must be there. The Decision paragraph is still exactly true under PRD v2 and is left alone. Ids are kept out because hsdd-config inlines every contract id an injected section names, which would push booking-api@v1 into the web and integration phases that only sign in.

question: ADR-001's Context says 'The PRD needs ...' and 'It fixes the API at two endpoints and rules out a database', which PRD v2 no longer does: rewrite the Context for PRD v2, name PRD 1 in it, or keep it as written?

options.label: Context as written, plus one pointer line to Amendments
options.consequence: The reasons of 2026-10-29 stay exactly as they were decided; a reader of Context meets a one-line note that PRD v2 changed its premises and where that is recorded. Context is never injected, so phase contexts are unaffected.

options.label: name PRD 1 in the Context sentences
options.consequence: The sentences become unambiguous about which PRD they describe, at the cost of editing the decision's recorded reasons in place.

options.label: rewrite Context for PRD v2
options.consequence: The Context would read as if the decision were taken for PRD v2, which rewrites the decision's history; the step's instructions forbid it.

chosen: Context as written, plus one pointer line to Amendments
why: The step's rule is to never rewrite the decision's history, and the ADR's date (2026-10-29) already places the Context before PRD v2. The pointer line adds without changing a word of the reasons, and the Amendments entry names what in the Context no longer holds (two endpoints, no database). DEC-015 expected H1 to rewrite 'The PRD needs' for content; this keeps it as history instead, and the cites-superseded experiment found no citation of a baseline path in ADR-001, so no citation touch is owed.

question: hsdd/management/2026-10-30-execution-plan.md routes C-2 (finding F-3): add simple-login to ADR-001's affects. Absorb it in this update and cite C-2, or leave it to that plan (Q-002, DEC-016)?

options.label: absorb C-2 here
options.consequence: affects gains simple-login in the same edit that adds booking-api@v1, one registry regeneration covers both, and the link is consistent both ways now (hsdd/spec/simple-login.md already carries Governed by: [ADR-001]). C-2's checkbox in the execution plan stays unticked until the next checkpoint reads the ADR; this step cannot edit a published plan.

options.label: leave C-2 to the execution plan
options.consequence: A second edit of the same affects line later, by the owner before Sync A, and the ADR's affects stays one-way until then.

chosen: absorb C-2 here
why: It is a link fix with no decision and no dependency (the execution plan's own words), on the exact line this step already changes. The root spec names ADR-001 under Governed by and proposed it in its Decisions section, so hsdd-adr's bidirectional rule wants simple-login in affects. Leaving it would only defer an identical edit. A pending spec touch that dropped Governed by from the root would have changed this, and H6 keeps ADR-001 among the root's decisions.

question: Adding governed_by: [ADR-001] to the front matter of auth-api@v1, profile-api@v1 and profile-api@v2 (Q-001): front matter only, or also a dated line in each contract's ## Versioning?

options.label: front matter only, version unchanged
options.consequence: Each file gains one front-matter line after owner, as hsdd-contract's template places it; the body's Governed by line, the Interface, the Guarantees, the schema and the fixtures stay as they are. The registry projects nothing from governed_by, so INDEX.md does not change. No Versioning line records it; git history does.

options.label: front matter plus a Versioning line
options.consequence: Each Versioning section, which records changes consumers can see, gains an entry for a link that changes nothing a consumer sees, and profile-api@v1, which waits on Sync A for its deprecation, gets an edit to its prose.

chosen: front matter only, version unchanged
why: The front-matter field is the contract's side of the link that hsdd-adr's affects requires, and the body line already said the same thing in the older shape; the change is metadata with no effect on the Interface, Guarantees or Validation, so under each contract's Versioning it is neither breaking nor an addition, and the version stays. Keeping profile-api@v1's prose untouched also leaves its pending deprecation (execution plan C-1) entirely to Sync A.

question: S03's report lists 19 reads outside its inputs (the integration spec and four verification docs, the open execution plan, conventions, three skills, hsdd-auto's scripts and S02's report). Keep the output or rework?

options.label: Keep the output
options.consequence: The ADR-001 amendment stands; the reads stay listed in the report for the review.

options.label: Rework without those reads
options.consequence: The step would decide the restart question without knowing which shipped phase relies on a restart for AC-2.3, which the intake record asked it to weigh.

chosen: Keep the output
why: The verification docs and the integration spec are where the record's H1 prompt sends the step (the AC-2.3 restart stand-in); the execution plan holds the C-2 repair the step absorbed; the rest is the run's own machinery. All are inside the repository and none is out of bounds. A read outside the repository would have changed this.

question: How do booking times travel on the wire, in requests and responses (PRD v2 AC-4.2, AC-5.1, AC-5.3, AC-6.1)?

options.label: UTC instants in toISOString form
options.consequence: Every instant is a UTC ISO-8601 string as Date.prototype.toISOString() writes it (2026-11-05T02:00:00.000Z), the same form as auth-api@v1's expiresAt fixture; one string per instant, so exact fixtures reproduce; every consumer converts to a zone before showing a time.

options.label: local times with the room's offset
options.consequence: 2026-11-05T09:00:00+07:00 reads naturally for the room's office, but several strings name one instant, an exact fixture depends on which offset the producer picks, and a London user's view still converts.

options.label: wall-clock date and times plus a zone name
options.consequence: { date, start: '01:30', zone } mirrors the form, but on London's October change day 01:30 names two instants, so the wire needs an offset as well, and every reader must resolve wall times.

chosen: UTC instants in toISOString form
why: An instant is the only form with one string per moment, which exact replay of fixtures needs, and it is what the existing contracts already carry (auth-api@v1 expiresAt '2026-10-29T10:30:00.000Z'). The experiment shows toISOString and JSON.stringify both write the .000Z form and that a date-time string without a zone parses as local time, which is why no other form is allowed on the wire. Wall-clock forms fail on the repeated hour of London's October change day (AC-4.4). A consumer that had to show times without any zone data would have favoured preformatted strings; the web app has the zone (AC-2.5).

question: How are booking times stored in PostgreSQL 17 (PRD v2 Constraints, AC-5.3, AC-5.4)?

options.label: timestamptz instants, half-open
options.consequence: start and end are timestamptz; a booking occupies [start, end), so touching bookings do not overlap and overlap is a comparison of instants that needs no zone; tstzrange(start, end, '[)') with && expresses it, and an exclusion constraint can hold AC-5.4 in the database. A change to a zone's rules would move a future booking's wall-clock time.

options.label: room-local wall time plus the room's zone
options.consequence: A future booking keeps its wall-clock time if a zone's rules change, but every overlap and 'started' check converts first, the repeated hour needs an offset column, and no plain exclusion constraint holds AC-5.4.

options.label: timestamp without time zone holding UTC
options.consequence: The same values on paper, but the column drops the Z it is given and its reading depends on the session TimeZone.

chosen: timestamptz instants, half-open
why: AC-5.3 (touching bookings do not overlap) and AC-5.4 (exactly one of two simultaneous overlapping bookings) are statements about instants. The experiment shows timestamptz reads back the same epoch whatever the session TimeZone, a timestamp column given the same '...Z' string reads back 7 hours apart under Asia/Jakarta and Europe/London sessions, '[)' ranges that touch do not overlap, and an exclusion constraint refuses the overlap with 23P01. Whether the backend uses that constraint is its own D{n} (DEC-010); this decision fixes only the type and the half-open rule. Jakarta has no daylight saving and London's rule is the long-standing last-Sunday rule, so rule changes are not a live risk for a laptop demo. Bookings kept years ahead in zones whose rules change often would have favoured storing the room's wall time beside the instant.

question: Where does the user's IANA time zone come from (PRD v2 AC-2.5)?

options.label: the account, served in the profile
options.consequence: The backend stores the zone with each built-in account (ayu Asia/Jakarta, budi Europe/London) and GET /api/me serves it as timeZone; the same user sees the same times on any machine; profile-api@v2 gains an optional field, which H5 classifies (DEC-007). The web app cannot show a time until the profile has loaded.

options.label: the browser's zone
options.consequence: No contract change, but Home would show the machine's zone rather than the account's, a user would see different times on two machines, and browser tests would depend on the zone of the machine running them.

chosen: the account, served in the profile
why: PRD v2 Demo accounts gives each account a time zone, and AC-2.1 lists the time zone among 'my details' on Home, beside the name and email the account already serves; AC-2.5 then says every time is in 'this zone', the one shown. The browser's zone is a property of the machine, and the experiment shows a resolved ambient zone can come back under another name than the one set (TZ=Asia/Kolkata resolves as Asia/Calcutta), so it is neither the account's nor stable to compare. A PRD asking for times in 'the zone of the computer I am using' would have led the other way.

question: Which node turns a date in the user's zone into a time range (AC-4.2), turns the booking form's date and times into instants (AC-5.1), and formats times, including the room's local times (AC-4.3) and the conflict message (AC-5.3)?

options.label: the web app converts both ways; the backend works in instants only
options.consequence: Every zone rule lives in one node, in pure functions that take the zone as an argument; the rooms query takes the day as two instants; overlap, started, ended, the quarter-hour rule and any limit are comparisons of instants, so the backend's tests on PostgreSQL need no clock-change cases. A second client would have to repeat the day-range rule.

options.label: the backend turns a date into a range; the web app formats
options.consequence: The query takes a date and the backend reads the account's zone, so the contract reads like the PRD; but zone arithmetic then lives in both nodes, and the form's wall times still need turning into instants, which on London's October change day needs an offset to pick one of the repeated hour's two instants.

options.label: the backend converts both ways and returns formatted strings
options.consequence: The web app shows strings, but the backend must format per user and per screen (the room's local times, the conflict message), and the web app cannot list the form's times for a date without asking the backend.

chosen: the web app converts both ways; the backend works in instants only
why: The web app must hold the user's zone anyway, to show it (AC-2.1, AC-2.5) and to format every time it shows (AC-2.5, AC-4.3, AC-5.3), so putting the reverse conversion in the same node keeps every zone rule in one set of pure functions, tested in isolation; the 23-hour and 25-hour London days the experiment computes are then a property of one function, not of two nodes that must agree. The backend's rules (AC-5.2 to AC-5.6, AC-6.1, AC-6.2) are all statements about instants. Both options keep the same nodes and the same contracts, so this is not a shape stop. A second consumer that queries by date, or a consumer that cannot hold the zone, would have favoured the backend turning dates into ranges.

question: Which clock decides that a booking has started (AC-5.5, AC-6.2) or ended (AC-6.1), and does a booking count as started at its start instant?

options.label: the backend's injected clock, started at the start instant
options.consequence: One authority, where the bookings are: started once the backend's clock reads the start or later, ended once it reads the end or later. The browser's clock only picks the date the Rooms screen opens on and may leave past times out of the form. Backend tests set the clock; end-to-end tests run under the real clock, so a started booking is hard to reach there.

options.label: the browser's clock, checked again by the backend
options.consequence: The form refuses early, but two clocks can disagree near a start, giving one answer on screen and another from the API; Playwright's mocked clock would change what the web app decides.

chosen: the backend's injected clock, started at the start instant
why: AC-5.5 and AC-6.2 are rules the backend must enforce whatever the client says, and AC-6.2's 'its time is free for anyone at once' is a database fact; ADR-001 already makes the backend's clock an injected dependency (Consequences: time is an input), so the same clock decides sessions and bookings. 'A time that has already started' includes the moment it starts, so equality counts as started; cancel is allowed only while the clock is before the start. A requirement that the form never offer a time the backend would refuse would have pushed the backend to publish its clock to the web app.

question: How does the quarter-hour rule (AC-5.2) stay right in the user's zone when the backend sees only instants?

options.label: check the UTC instant
options.consequence: The backend accepts a time only when its UTC minutes are a multiple of 15 and its seconds and milliseconds are zero; this equals the rule on the user's wall clock while every zone offset is a multiple of 15 minutes, and needs no zone in the backend.

options.label: convert to the user's zone and check there
options.consequence: Exact for any zone, including one with an offset that is not a multiple of 15 minutes, but brings zone arithmetic into the backend for a case the time-zone data does not contain.

chosen: check the UTC instant
why: The experiment found no zone among the 418 Node.js 24 knows (tz data 2026b) whose offset is anything but a multiple of 15 minutes from 2026 to 2028, sampled every 6 hours, and every quarter-hour slot of London's two change days is a quarter hour both in UTC and on London's wall clock. The demo's two zones are whole hours from UTC. An account in a zone with an offset that is not a multiple of 15 minutes would have forced the check into the user's zone.

question: How does the booking form handle London's clock-change days (AC-4.4, AC-5.1): the hour the clocks skip in March and the hour they repeat in October?

options.label: offer the day's quarter-hour instants
options.consequence: The form's times for a date are every quarter-hour instant from the start of that day up to the start of the next, labelled with its wall-clock time: on the March day 01:00 to 01:45 never appear, on the October day they appear twice, once per instant. No wall time is ever resolved by a rule, and the web app needs a label that tells the two apart.

options.label: offer 00:00 to 23:45 and refuse a skipped or repeated time
options.consequence: A fixed list, but on two days a year the user meets an error for a time the form offered, and nobody can book the repeated hour at all.

options.label: offer 00:00 to 23:45 and resolve by rule
options.consequence: No error (a skipped time moves later, a repeated one takes the earlier instant), but a booking can land at a time the user did not pick, and the second 01:30 cannot be chosen.

chosen: offer the day's quarter-hour instants
why: Enumerating instants makes the form agree with the day range of AC-4.2 by construction: the experiment lists 92 slots on 2027-03-28 with no 01:xx and 100 on 2027-10-31 with 01:00 to 01:45 twice (BST, then GMT), every one a quarter hour. AC-4.4 asks for times that are right on those days, which rules out a time that does not exist and a silent move. If the PRD had said bookings never fall between 01:00 and 02:00 on a Sunday, the fixed list would have been enough.

question: How are times shown where PRD v2's examples are silent: a time that falls on another date than the one its line is about, and a wall time in the hour London's clocks repeat?

options.label: carry the date; mark the repeated hour with the zone's short name
options.consequence: A London booking from 16:00 to 19:00 on 5 November reads '23:00 to Fri 6 Nov 02:00' for a Jakarta user; October's two 01:30s read '01:30 BST' and '01:30 GMT'. Every line is unambiguous, and the web app and the integration node assert the same strings.

options.label: times only, as PRD v2's examples show them
options.consequence: Shorter, but the same booking reads '23:00 to 02:00' with no hint of the next day, and the two 01:30s look identical, on a day AC-4.4 says must be right.

options.label: always show the UTC offset
options.consequence: Unambiguous, but every line carries an offset that PRD v2's examples do not show, and the AC-4.3 and AC-5.3 strings no longer match the PRD.

chosen: carry the date; mark the repeated hour with the zone's short name
why: Jakarta and London are 7 or 8 hours apart, so a booking in one office regularly crosses midnight in the other, and AC-4.2 lists bookings that merely overlap the picked date. PRD v2's examples ('09:00 to 10:00', 'Thu 5 Nov', 'Merapi is already booked from 10:00 to 11:00.') stay exact on ordinary lines because both marks appear only when needed. The experiment shows en-GB's short names are GMT and BST for London (en-US gives GMT+1) and en-GB writes 'Thu 5 Nov' with HH:mm on a 23-hour clock. The rule sits in the ADR rather than the web app's D{n} because the integration node asserts these strings and cannot read the web app's phase plan. A PRD rule limiting bookings to office hours would have made the date mark unnecessary.

question: Where does a booking show the room's local times (AC-4.3), and how is 'another time zone than mine' tested?

options.label: on the Rooms screen, when the zone names differ
options.consequence: A plain comparison of two names the backend serves (the room's timeZone and the account's timeZone); Home and the conflict message show the user's zone only. A user in a zone that shares the room's offset would still see the room's times.

options.label: on the Rooms screen, when the offsets differ at the booking's start
options.consequence: Hides a parenthetical that would repeat the same times, but whether a line has one then depends on the date for zones with different daylight-saving rules, and tests must compute offsets.

options.label: wherever a booking appears
options.consequence: Home's My bookings and the conflict message also carry the room's times, which PRD v2's AC-5.3 example and Home sketch do not show.

chosen: on the Rooms screen, when the zone names differ
why: AC-4.3 sits under US-4, the Rooms screen, and says 'another time zone than mine', which names a zone, not an offset; AC-5.3's example message and the Home sketch carry no room times. Both names come from the backend (the account and the room), so the comparison never involves the runtime's own spelling of a zone. Demo users whose zones share an offset with a room's office would have made the offset comparison worth its cost.

question: Do the tests of every node that handles time run in an ambient time zone that is neither account's nor UTC, or is that left to each node's plan?

options.label: required in every node's tests
options.consequence: TZ for the Node.js test runners and the browser's time zone for the browser tests are set to a third zone, for example Asia/Kolkata (+05:30), so a time computed in the ambient zone fails a test; each gate gains one setting.

options.label: left to each node's plan
options.consequence: No cross-node rule; tests run in the laptop's zone, so on a laptop set to Asia/Jakarta a time computed in the ambient zone is right for Ayu and the bug passes.

chosen: required in every node's tests
why: Decision items 3 and 4 say no node uses the ambient zone; only a test run in a zone that differs from both accounts' and from UTC can show it, and the experiment shows TZ changes the ambient zone of a Node.js process (Asia/Kolkata gives getHours() 7 for 02:00Z). A half-hour offset also makes a stray ambient-zone time land off the quarter hour. The integration node cannot read the web app's plan, so a rule both must follow belongs here. If every developer's laptop ran in UTC, the risk would be smaller but not gone: UTC hides the same bug for budi in winter.

question: Does ADR-002's affects name the root simple-login beside the five targets the intake record lists (simple-login.backend, simple-login.web, simple-login.integration, profile-api@v2, booking-api@v1)?

options.label: add simple-login
options.consequence: The root's header gains ADR-002 under Governed by now, so the link is two-way when H6 makes ADR-002 one of the root's Decisions, as ADR-001's is; H6 must keep the line when it restates the header.

options.label: the five targets only
options.consequence: As the intake record lists them; the root names ADR-002 only in its Decisions section, and if H6 also lists it under Governed by, ADR-002's affects is one-way, the finding F-3 raised for ADR-001.

chosen: add simple-login
why: H6 adds ADR-002 to the root's Decisions section, and PRD v2's Goal that every time on screen is in the user's zone is a root-level constraint this ADR carries out across all three children. The checkpoint's finding F-3 (execution plan C-2) and DEC-022 settled that a root which names an ADR in its header and Decisions belongs in that ADR's affects. The intake record's list names where the work lands, not the root's link. If H6's prompt had kept ADR-002 out of the root's Decisions, the five targets would have been enough.

question: Where does the link to ADR-002 go: node headers only, or also the root's embedded child summaries and every phase header; and in profile-api@v2, the front matter only or also the body's Governed by line?

options.label: node headers and their embedded copies; both lines in profile-api@v2; no phase headers
options.consequence: Four node headers and the root's three embedded summaries name ADR-002; profile-api@v2's governed_by and body line both read [ADR-001, ADR-002], a metadata change that keeps v2 with no Versioning line; every existing phase has shipped and keeps its header, and the new phases take ADR-002 from their own plans (H14, H16, H18).

options.label: also every phase header
options.consequence: Marks shipped history with a decision taken after it shipped, and edits nine phases whose verification docs are on the main line.

options.label: node files only, front matter only
options.consequence: The root's embedded summaries and profile-api@v2's body line keep saying [ADR-001] while the headers and front matter say more: a drift H5 and H7 to H9 would have to notice.

chosen: node headers and their embedded copies; both lines in profile-api@v2; no phase headers
why: hsdd-adr asks for Governed by on every affected node and contract; the root's embedded summaries are copies of the child headers and nothing but this step adds the line to them. profile-api@v2's two Governed by lines said the same thing until now; keeping them equal follows DEC-023, which classed governed_by as metadata that changes no Interface, Guarantee or Validation and so keeps the version. No shipped phase was governed by a decision taken today, and hsdd-adr's citation-touch rule keeps a shipped phase as history. simple-login.integration had no Governed by line, so it gains one after Produces, where the other nodes carry it. A spec touch that rewrote the embedded summaries from the child files would have made the copies redundant here.

question: Materializing an ADR whose decision no human stated

options.label: write it accepted, its Context citing this decision
options.consequence: ADR-002 binds from now: hsdd-config injects its Decision and Consequences into every phase it governs, and H3, H5 and the phase plans build on it; the rule 'never write invented content as accepted' gives way, and the owner's review of DEC-025 to DEC-036 is the human act.

options.label: write it proposed with the Decision as a TODO
options.consequence: Nothing invented binds, but booking-api@v1 (H3), the profile touch (H5) and every phase plan would be drafted against an open time model, and the owner asked not to be asked in this segment.

chosen: write it accepted, its Context citing this decision
why: hsdd-adr's Unattended runs table disposes this ask point as 'decide: write it accepted' with class judgement, and the run's decision policy covers accepting proposed ADRs. The owner asked for every question to be decided and recorded for one review sitting. The decision itself rests on PRD v2's acceptance criteria and two experiments, and each of its choices is recorded separately (DEC-025 to DEC-036). A careful engineer would still have shown the owner a time model before binding three nodes to it, hence would_have_asked.

question: S04's report lists reads outside its inputs (the open execution plan, earlier step reports, conventions, auth-api's contract, schema and a fixture, the three package.json files, hsdd-config and the run's scripts). Keep the output or rework?

options.label: Keep the output
options.consequence: ADR-002 stands; the reads stay listed for the review.

options.label: Rework without those reads
options.consequence: The time model would be decided without auth-api's existing instant format (expiresAt) and without the toolchain versions its experiments checked, so it could pick a wire format that disagrees with the shipped contract.

chosen: Keep the output
why: auth-api's expiresAt format is the precedent DEC-025 follows; the package files fix the Node version the Intl experiment ran on; the rest is the run's own machinery. All are inside the repository; none is out of bounds. A read outside the repository would have changed this.

question: Which compatibility does booking-api@v1 declare: additive-only, versioned or frozen?

options.label: versioned
options.consequence: The default. A compatible addition keeps v1; a breaking change (a tighter limit, a new refusal, a changed code) drafts v2 with a migration note. The limits and the conflict rule can still be revised later through a bump.

options.label: additive-only
options.consequence: Promises v1 only ever gains optional fields. Any later change to a limit, a code or the conflict rule would need a new contract or a redesign, and every existing fixture must stay valid under every amendment.

options.label: frozen
options.consequence: For interfaces not under the tree's control; booking-api is designed here and owned by simple-login.backend, so it does not fit.

chosen: versioned
why: booking-api@v1 states two limits PRD v2 leaves to engineering and a rule for which booking a refusal names; those are the parts most likely to change once people use it, and each change is breaking for a consumer that tests it. versioned keeps a v2 path for them, where additive-only would forbid it. profile-api@v2 took additive-only because one endpoint serves one shape that only grows; booking-api has four endpoints with refusal rules. If PRD v2 had fixed both limits, additive-only would have been as good.

question: Which endpoints carry PRD v2 US-4 to US-6: every room with its bookings on a date, booking a room, my bookings, cancelling one?

options.label: four endpoints: GET /api/rooms?from&to, GET /api/me/bookings, POST /api/bookings, DELETE /api/bookings/{id}
options.consequence: One endpoint per story action. The rooms view takes the day as two instants (ADR-002), my bookings sits beside GET /api/me, and a cancel answers 204 with no body. Four route fixtures sets for the web's stub to match on method and path.

options.label: GET /api/bookings with filters (?mine, ?from&to) plus POST and DELETE
options.consequence: One list endpoint whose meaning changes with its query; the rooms view would need a second call for the rooms themselves, and a filter combination would need its own rules.

options.label: cancel as POST /api/bookings/{id}/cancel returning the booking
options.consequence: Keeps a cancelled booking addressable and returns it, but nothing in PRD v2 shows a cancelled booking again; it adds a state to the Booking shape.

chosen: four endpoints: GET /api/rooms?from&to, GET /api/me/bookings, POST /api/bookings, DELETE /api/bookings/{id}
why: Each PRD v2 action maps to one request with one meaning. The rooms view returns every room with its bookings, as AC-4.1 and AC-4.2 show them on one screen, so the web needs one call per date; ADR-002 Decision 4 fixes its query as two instants. GET /api/me/bookings scopes to the token's account the way GET /api/me does, so no request names another user. DELETE answers 204: AC-6.2 says the booking leaves the list and nothing shows it again. Every endpoint takes the bearer token (ADR-001). If a consumer needed rooms without bookings, a separate GET /api/rooms without a range would have led.

question: What shape does a booking take in the rooms view, my bookings, a created booking and the overlap refusal?

options.label: one flat Booking { id, roomId, roomName, title, start, end } everywhere
options.consequence: One type for every response; Home can show the room's name without loading the rooms (AC-6.1), and the overlap refusal carries the room's name ADR-002 asks for. In the rooms view roomId and roomName repeat the enclosing room.

options.label: a Booking nested under its room in the rooms view, and a second shape with a room reference elsewhere
options.consequence: No repetition in the rooms view, but two booking types for consumers to write and keep apart, the split DEC-006 rejected between contracts.

options.label: a Booking with roomId only, and the room list sent beside each list
options.consequence: No repetition, but my bookings and the refusal carry a room list too, and every consumer joins the two.

chosen: one flat Booking { id, roomId, roomName, title, start, end } everywhere
why: DEC-006 put US-4 to US-6 in one contract because all of them show the same booking; one flat type keeps that true inside the contract. AC-6.1 lists my bookings with the room, and ADR-002 Decision 7 has Home and the overlap message show the room's name only, so roomName is all those consumers need; the rooms view's full room (office, timeZone, seats) stays on the room. The booking carries no account identity: no PRD v2 criterion shows who booked, and the rooms view is visible to every user. Room ids are lower-case slugs of the names (merapi, bromo, thames, kew), readable in fixtures and stable because rooms are never managed in the app (PRD v2 Rooms). A requirement to show who booked a room would have added an owner field.

question: What form does a booking id take on the wire?

options.label: a lower-case UUID string
options.consequence: PostgreSQL 17 generates it (gen_random_uuid), it is safe in a URL path without encoding, and the producer's replay can seed a fixture's given bookings with the fixture's own ids, so exact replay needs no id mapping. It constrains the producer to UUIDs.

options.label: an opaque string of URL-safe characters
options.consequence: Leaves the producer free (serial, UUID, other), but the replay must map fixture ids to the producer's ids in paths and bodies, or the producer must store any id a seed gives it.

options.label: an integer
options.consequence: Short and sortable, but enumerable and a JSON number, and seeding fixture ids needs sequence handling.

chosen: a lower-case UUID string
why: Fixtures must replay exactly against a stateful producer: the given bookings of a fixture are seeded with fixed ids, and the cancel and conflict fixtures name them. A UUID lets the seed use the fixture's ids as they are, in a uuid column, with no mapping rule in the contract. A created booking's id is new and is checked by pattern only. An id is never reused, so a cancelled booking's id answers 404. If the backend had already chosen integer keys, the opaque-string option with an id map would have led.

question: Which error codes do consumers branch on, with which statuses and messages?

options.label: eight codes, one per case a consumer treats differently, each with a fixed message
options.consequence: UNAUTHORIZED 401, VALIDATION_FAILED 400, BOOKING_TOO_LONG 422, BOOKING_STARTED 422, BOOKING_TOO_FAR_AHEAD 422, BOOKING_CONFLICT 409, BOOKING_NOT_FOUND 404, BOOKING_NOT_YOURS 403. The web can say why a booking was refused without parsing a message; fixed messages keep every error fixture exact.

options.label: a few coarse codes (VALIDATION_FAILED, CONFLICT, FORBIDDEN, NOT_FOUND) with explanatory messages
options.consequence: Fewer codes, but the web could not tell a started time from a too-long one without reading error.message, which every contract here forbids; varying messages make error fixtures schema-only.

options.label: a distinct code for every validation rule (quarter hour, end before start, title, unknown room)
options.consequence: Finer reporting, but the web's form already prevents each of those, so the codes would only ever reach a consumer with a bug.

chosen: eight codes, one per case a consumer treats differently, each with a fixed message
why: A code earns its place when a consumer acts on it differently. UNAUTHORIZED keeps profile-api@v2's body, the one 401 case ADR-001 Consequences asks for at every endpoint. BOOKING_CONFLICT carries the booking the web needs for AC-5.3's message. BOOKING_STARTED covers AC-5.5 and AC-6.2's started case at both endpoints, because ADR-002 Decision 5 defines started once. The two limit codes let the web explain the limits engineering chose. BOOKING_NOT_FOUND tells a second tab that its cancel already happened; BOOKING_NOT_YOURS is AC-6.3. The form-level rules (AC-5.2, AC-5.6, an unknown room, a malformed range) share VALIDATION_FAILED: the web prevents them before sending, as it does for AC-1.3. 409 marks a clash with another booking; 422 marks a well-formed request a rule refuses. If the web had needed to highlight the faulty field, per-rule validation codes would have led.

question: Where does the overlap refusal carry the room's name and the other booking's start and end, given RFC-001 §2's one error envelope { error: { code, message } }?

options.label: inside the envelope, as error.conflict, present only with BOOKING_CONFLICT
options.consequence: Every error still parses as the envelope; one code gains one documented field holding a Booking. The 'no other fields' line of auth-api and profile-api is not repeated here.

options.label: beside the envelope, as a top-level conflict field
options.consequence: The error object keeps exactly code and message, but the body is no longer just the envelope, and consumers read two places for one error.

options.label: only in error.message, as a preformatted sentence
options.consequence: No new field, but the message would be in a zone the backend does not know (ADR-002 Decision 4), and consumers would parse a message they must never branch on.

chosen: inside the envelope, as error.conflict, present only with BOOKING_CONFLICT
why: ADR-002 Decision 7 and its Consequences require the refusal to carry the other booking's start and end as instants and the room's name, so the web writes AC-5.3's message in the user's zone. RFC-001 §2 fixes the envelope's two fields but does not forbid more; extending the error object keeps one parse path for every error. The field holds the same Booking shape as every other response (DEC-041), so its title is no more exposed than in the rooms view. A consumer library that rejected unknown error fields would have favoured the top-level option.

question: Which other booking does the overlap refusal name when a request overlaps several (Q-010 (2))?

options.label: the overlapping booking with the earliest start
options.consequence: Deterministic and exactly replayable; the producer re-reads the room's overlapping bookings after the refusal (the exclusion constraint's 23P01 DETAIL names one row, not necessarily this one) and answers with the first by start.

options.label: whichever booking the database reports
options.consequence: No re-read, but the answer depends on index order, so a fixture with two overlaps can only replay by schema, and the web's message could name a later booking than the first clash.

options.label: every overlapping booking
options.consequence: Complete, but AC-5.3's message names one booking, and a list field makes the refusal's shape differ from every other Booking use.

chosen: the overlapping booking with the earliest start
why: AC-5.3's message names one other booking, and the earliest is the first clash a user would see scanning the day. The experiment behind ADR-002 shows the exclusion constraint's DETAIL names one conflicting row with no ordering promise, so the rule needs a re-read whatever the producer's mechanism (DEC-010 leaves that to the backend). Within one room live bookings never overlap each other, so their starts are distinct and the rule picks exactly one. A 409 always names a live booking that overlaps the request when the producer answers; if the re-read finds none because the clash was cancelled meanwhile, the producer tries the request again rather than answer 409 without one. If AC-5.3 had listed every clash, the list option would have led.

question: PRD v2 Left to engineering: the longest booking allowed, if there is a limit.

options.label: 8 hours of elapsed time
options.consequence: A working day fits in one booking; a mistaken hold of a room overnight or for days is refused with BOOKING_TOO_LONG. A 9-hour workshop takes two touching bookings. On London's October change day a wall-clock span crossing 01:00 to 02:00 counts the extra hour.

options.label: 12 hours of elapsed time
options.consequence: Any long working day fits, and multi-day holds are still refused; a 12-hour hold overnight would pass.

options.label: no limit
options.consequence: One code fewer; the web's form already keeps a booking within one date (ADR-002 Decision 4), but a script or a later client could hold a room for weeks.

chosen: 8 hours of elapsed time
why: PRD v2 is about meeting rooms booked in under a minute, and its problem statement is double bookings and misread times, not long events, so the limit's job is to refuse mistakes rather than ration rooms. 8 hours holds a whole working day, and touching bookings do not overlap (AC-5.3), so a longer event remains possible as two bookings. ADR-002 Consequences make the limit a comparison of instants, so the backend needs no zone. The limit is stated in the contract because consumers see it (DEC-011). A product statement about all-day workshops or training days would have moved this to 12 hours or no limit.

question: PRD v2 Left to engineering: how far ahead a room can be booked, if there is a limit (Q-010 (1): with a smaller limit the integration node cannot always book on the next clock-change day through the API under the real clock).

options.label: a start at most 365 days after the backend's clock
options.consequence: Every London clock-change instant is at most 217 days after any clock (experiment), so the next change day is always bookable through the API under the real clock, with about 147 days of margin; it bounds how far a zone-rule change can move a stored booking (ADR-002 Consequences).

options.label: 90 or 180 days
options.consequence: A shorter planning window, but for part of every year the next change day lies beyond it, so the integration node would need a backend clock hook or direct seeding to reach AC-4.4 under the real clock; direct seeding would make the database cross-node (DEC-010).

options.label: no limit
options.consequence: The change days are always reachable and there is one code fewer, but a booking can be made decades ahead, beyond any assumption about zone rules.

chosen: a start at most 365 days after the backend's clock
why: ADR-002 Consequences tie this limit to whether the integration node can book on the next clock-change day through the API; the experiment scans every hour from 2026-10-31 to 2031 and finds the next change instant at most 217.00 days ahead (worst clock 2027-03-28T01:00Z), and from today 147 days. 180 days fails that, 365 passes it with room, and a year is a limit a user reads without explanation. It is measured as elapsed time (8,760 hours) on the start, a comparison of instants as ADR-002 requires. Boundary: a start exactly 365 days after the clock is accepted. A product wish for a short planning window would have favoured 90 days plus a test-only clock in the backend.

question: When a request breaks more than one rule, which refusal does it get?

options.label: a fixed order: 401, then 400, then BOOKING_TOO_LONG, BOOKING_STARTED, BOOKING_TOO_FAR_AHEAD, then 409; for a cancel 401, 404, 403, then BOOKING_STARTED
options.consequence: Every request has exactly one answer, so fixtures replay exactly and the integration node can assert one code; rules that need no state come before rules that read the clock, and the overlap check, which reads the database, comes last.

options.label: leave the order to the producer
options.consequence: Less to state, but a request that is both started and overlapping could get either code, so such cases cannot be fixtures and the web's message for them is unpredictable.

chosen: a fixed order: 401, then 400, then BOOKING_TOO_LONG, BOOKING_STARTED, BOOKING_TOO_FAR_AHEAD, then 409; for a cancel 401, 404, 403, then BOOKING_STARTED
why: A contract that both sides test exactly needs one answer per request. The order goes from what needs nothing (the token, the request's form, the length) to what needs the clock (started, how far ahead) to what needs other bookings (the overlap), which is also the cheapest order for the producer. For a cancel, ownership comes before the clock so that a user learns nothing about the timing of a booking that is not theirs beyond its existence, which the rooms view shows anyway. A started time that also overlaps gets BOOKING_STARTED: booking it again later cannot help, while a conflict suggests another time might. If the web had wanted to show every broken rule at once, a list of codes would have led.

question: AC-5.6 says the title is required and at most 80 characters: what counts as a character, is a blank title 'given', and is the title trimmed?

options.label: 1 to 80 code points with at least one non-whitespace character, stored and returned exactly as sent
options.consequence: Matches auth-api@v1's definition of a character (what JSON Schema's maxLength counts), refuses a title of spaces, and keeps what the producer returns equal to what was sent, so fixtures replay exactly. The web trims before sending if it wants trimmed titles.

options.label: trim, then require 1 to 80 code points
options.consequence: Friendlier to sloppy input, but the returned title differs from the request, the length rule applies to a string the client never sent, and the schema cannot express it.

options.label: 1 to 80 UTF-16 units, blanks allowed
options.consequence: What a JavaScript length check gives, but it disagrees with the schema's maxLength for emoji and lets an empty-looking title through.

chosen: 1 to 80 code points with at least one non-whitespace character, stored and returned exactly as sent
why: 'Required' is read as having something to show: a title of spaces would list as blank on Home and the Rooms screen. auth-api@v1 already defines a character as a Unicode code point after both sides met the ambiguity, and the same definition lets the schema state the rule (minLength, maxLength and a non-whitespace pattern). Storing the title as sent follows auth-api@v1's no-trimming rule for usernames. A fixture with an 80-code-point title of 81 UTF-16 units pins the definition. A PRD criterion about trimming would have led to the second option.

question: Which ranges does GET /api/rooms accept, and which instant strings does any request accept?

options.label: from and to in exactly the toISOString form, from before to, no cap on the range's length
options.consequence: One string per instant in both directions (ADR-002 Decision 1), so '2026-11-05T00:00:00Z' without milliseconds or any offset is a 400; a day of 23, 24 or 25 hours needs no special case, and a test may query a wider range to inspect state.

options.label: the same, with the range capped at 48 hours
options.consequence: Bounds a response's size, but adds a refusal no PRD v2 criterion needs on a laptop with four rooms, and one more rule to keep in step with the web's day arithmetic.

options.label: accept any ISO-8601 instant with an offset, normalising it
options.consequence: Lenient for scripts, but several strings name one instant, so request fixtures and the web's stub matching are no longer one-to-one, which ADR-002 rejected.

chosen: from and to in exactly the toISOString form, from before to, no cap on the range's length
why: ADR-002 Decision 1 says no other form crosses the wire, and its experiment shows a string without a zone parses as local time, so the producer accepts a string only when it equals the toISOString of the instant it names (which also refuses impossible dates). The web sends one day, at most 25 hours (ADR-002 Decision 4); nothing in PRD v2 needs a cap, and with four rooms the size is small. A query value may be sent with its colons percent-encoded or not; the producer decodes both, so the web can build it with URLSearchParams. A deployment beyond the laptop would have favoured a cap.

question: In which order do the rooms and the booking lists come back, when 'earliest first' and 'soonest first' leave ties?

options.label: rooms in PRD v2 Rooms' order; bookings by start, ties broken by the rooms' order
options.consequence: Every list has one order, so exact replay works and the web renders what it receives without sorting. Within one room starts never tie, because live bookings of a room do not overlap; across rooms (my bookings) two of mine may start together, and the room order settles it.

options.label: rooms by name; bookings by start, ties by booking id
options.consequence: Also total, but alphabetical rooms split each office's rooms (Bromo, Kew, Merapi, Thames), and an id tie-break is random to a reader.

options.label: order left unspecified; consumers sort
options.consequence: Less to promise, but every consumer writes the same sort, and fixtures need order-insensitive comparison.

chosen: rooms in PRD v2 Rooms' order; bookings by start, ties broken by the rooms' order
why: AC-4.2 says earliest first and AC-6.1 soonest first; both read as by start. PRD v2 Rooms and its Screens list Merapi, Bromo, Thames, Kew, grouped by office, so that is the rooms' order. A total order lets both sides replay fixtures exactly and keeps sorting out of the web. If rooms were managed in the app, a stored sort key would have replaced the PRD's order.

question: How do booking-api@v1's fixtures carry the state and the clock a booking request depends on, so the producer's gate can replay them and consumers can stub with them?

options.label: each fixture adds clock and given to the existing format
options.consequence: clock is the instant the producer's injected clock reads; given lists the bookings that exist first, with fixed ids, owners and times, seeded directly (some lie before the clock, which the API would refuse). Requests and responses stay as in auth-api and profile-api, the token placeholders keep their meaning, and consumers keep using only request and response. The backend's replay rig grows a seed and a clock hook.

options.label: scenario fixtures: a sequence of requests per file
options.consequence: Can express 'cancel, then the time is free' and the 20-attempt race, but consumers' stubs answer one call per route, and the existing rig and fetch stub would both need a new runner.

options.label: single requests with no state; stateful cases replay by schema only
options.consequence: No rig changes, but the overlap, conflict-naming, started and my-bookings rules would not be checked by any fixture.

chosen: each fixture adds clock and given to the existing format
why: The guarantees that matter most here (touching versus overlapping, which booking a refusal names, started at equality, what my bookings hold) depend on existing bookings and the clock; without both, those fixtures could not replay exactly. Adding two fields keeps the format the backend's rig and the web's stub already read (backend/test/replay.ts; web/src/test/fetchStub.ts matches on method and path), and the backend already injects its clock (ADR-001, ADR-002 Decision 5). Sequence properties stay out of fixtures: exactly one of simultaneous requests (G5), a cancelled time being free at once, and bookings surviving a restart are proven by the producer's tests and the integration node. A 201's id is the one value a fixture cannot predict; it is checked against the schema and must differ from every given id. If a consumer needed to stub a multi-call flow from one file, scenario fixtures would have led.

question: Which provisional ids go in produced_by and consumers before any phase plan names booking-api@v1?

options.label: the next phase of each leaf-parent: simple-login.backend.4, simple-login.web.5, simple-login.integration.3
options.consequence: Follows hsdd-contract's 'first phase of each leaf-parent' guess for an append; gate C7 warns (not errors) while those headings do not exist, and hsdd-reconcile replaces them with the confirmed ids.

options.label: the node ids: simple-login.backend, simple-login.web, simple-login.integration
options.consequence: No C7 warning, but the skill reserves node ids for adopted nodes that have no phases yet; these nodes have phases.

chosen: the next phase of each leaf-parent: simple-login.backend.4, simple-login.web.5, simple-login.integration.3
why: hsdd-contract says produced_by and consumers usually start as the first phase of each leaf-parent, marked phase_ids: provisional; for nodes that already have phases 1 to 3, 1 to 4 and 1 to 2, the first appended phase is the guess. The appends (H14, H16, H18) may give the work to a later phase; their confirm entries settle it at reconcile. The warning is expected until then.
evidence: .claude/skills/hsdd-contract/SKILL.md Provisional Phase Ids and the Writer Rule

question: What does booking-api@v1's Breaking: line count as breaking, in particular a change to either limit?

options.label: any change to either limit, in either direction, is breaking
options.consequence: A limit is a stated guarantee that fixtures pin (book-eight-hours, book-too-long, book-365-days-ahead, book-too-far-ahead) and that the web's form and the integration tests may rely on; loosening it fails their assertions as surely as tightening breaks requests. Every limit change drafts v2.

options.label: only tightening a limit is breaking; loosening is a compatible amendment
options.consequence: Fewer bumps if the limits prove too tight, but an amendment in place would change two fixtures' outcomes and the consumers' tests that assert the refusal, which hsdd-contract's 'if a consumer's code could break, it is a new version' forbids.

chosen: any change to either limit, in either direction, is breaking
why: hsdd-contract's anti-rationalization table says a change that could break a consumer's code is a new version, and the integration node's tests assert the refusals at the boundaries. The same reasoning covers the check order and which booking error.conflict names. Compatible changes stay narrow: a new optional response field (consumers ignore unknown fields), a new endpoint, a new pre-loaded room (consumers render the list they receive). If the consumers had promised never to assert a limit, loosening could have been compatible.

question: S05's report lists reads outside its inputs (earlier step records and experiments, the backend's replay rig and the web's fetch stub with their tests, the package files). Keep the output or rework?

options.consequence: booking-api@v1 stands; its fixtures are shaped so the existing replay rig and fetch stub can be extended to them, and the routed items name the gaps.

options.label: Rework without those reads
options.consequence: The fixtures would be designed blind to the rigs that replay them; the 204 and query-encoding gaps would surface only when a phase runs.

All reads are inside the repository; none is out of bounds. A read outside the repository would have changed this.

question: hsdd/management/2026-10-30-execution-plan.md routes C-3 (finding F-4): add the web phases that read auth-api@v1's fixtures to its consumers. Absorb it in this touch and cite C-3, or leave it to that plan (Q-003, DEC-016)?

C-3's other half, whether the shipped phases' Consumes lines in hsdd/spec/simple-login.web.md are corrected or left with a note, is a spec question this skill never edits and stays with the owner. The facts check out in the repository: web/src/App.test.tsx line 85 stubs fetch with auth-api's login-success fixture for the walk, web.3's verification doc says it consumes auth-api@v1 for the sign-in step, and web.4's says the web.3 walk passes unchanged on the v2 fixtures. A shipped phase stays in consumers until it migrates to a later version, as web.1 and web.2 do, so both belong there. It follows DEC-016's routing and matches DEC-022, which absorbed C-2 the same way. A sign that C-3's owner question about the Consumes lines had to be answered first (for example a check that a consumers entry must appear in the phase's Consumes line) would have left it to the plan; gate check C7 asks only that the phase heading exists.

question: How do auth-api@v1's guarantees follow ADR-001 as updated on a restart, and how does that change classify against auth-api@v1's Versioning?

options.label: a restart guarantee of its own, classified as a clarification
options.consequence: The token guarantee keeps 'accepted until expiresAt, and rejected after it' and points to a new guarantee: a restart ends every token issued before it, and each is then rejected exactly as an expired token is (ADR-001). Phase gates and the integration node's restart test can cite it by id. The version stays v1: the behavior is the one ADR-001 has stated since 2026-10-29 and the shipped service has always had.

options.label: leave the token guarantee as written
options.consequence: No edit for the restart; ADR-001's Consequences carry it. The contract keeps a sentence that a restart makes false, which a consumer reading only the contract, as HSDD intends, would take at its word.

options.label: treat the restart wording as a narrowed guarantee, v2
options.consequence: auth-api@v2 with a migration note and its own schema and fixtures, identical in shape to v1, and a breaking-amend stop for a stable versioned contract. Every consumer node would need a phase to move to a version that changes no byte on the wire.

chosen: a restart guarantee of its own, classified as a clarification
why: The invocation asks the guarantees to follow ADR-001 on a restart. ADR-001's first Consequences bullet has said 'Restarting the backend signs every user out' since its first version (commit e84ae36), its 2026-10-31 amendment keeps sessions in memory (DEC-018), and backend/src/sessions.ts holds tokens in a per-process Map. No consumer could rely on a token outliving a restart: simple-login.integration.1 and .2 rely on the opposite, using a restart as the expired-token stand-in for AC-2.3. So the change is a wording fix that makes the text match behavior v1 always had, like the 2026-10-30 code-point entry, and the skill's test 'if a consumer's code could break, it is a new version' finds no consumer to break. A separate guarantee rather than a clause in the token guarantee lets PRD v2's restart tests cite it. A shipped consumer whose code or tests assumed a token survives a restart would have made this a breaking change and a stop.

question: Does auth-api@v1 state sign-out as a guarantee, now that ADR-001's update keeps it client-side with no logout endpoint (DEC-019), and how does that classify?

options.label: a sign-out guarantee, classified as a clarification
options.consequence: One guarantee: sign-out is client-side, there is no logout endpoint, a client signs out by discarding its token, and a token kept or copied before sign-out stays accepted until it expires or the service restarts. A consumer reading only the contract learns there is nothing to call and what the exposure is. No endpoint, shape or fixture changes, so v1 stays. A later logout endpoint would be an addition that leaves a client that never calls it unaffected.

options.label: leave sign-out to ADR-001
options.consequence: The contract stays silent; hsdd-config still injects ADR-001's Decision and Consequences into every phase it governs. A reader of the contract alone cannot tell whether a logout call exists or was forgotten, and the booking phases learn that a copied token can book and cancel only from the ADR.

chosen: a sign-out guarantee, classified as a clarification
why: The invocation asks the guarantees to follow ADR-001 on sign-out, and a contract is meant to be the one thing a consumer needs. RFC-001 §3 and ADR-001 have made sign-out client-side since v1 and DEC-019 kept it; the shipped backend has only POST /api/login and GET /api/me (backend/src/routes.ts), and the web's sign-out discards its token. So the guarantee describes behavior v1 always had and adds no rule a consumer must change for. Worded as 'signing out ends nothing on the service' rather than 'nothing can ever revoke a token', it does not bind the producer against a later revocation endpoint. A PRD v2 criterion on shared devices or a deployment beyond one laptop (root OQ1) would have argued for a revocation endpoint instead, which is DEC-019's question, not this one.

question: auth-api@v1's guarantees carry no ids, while hsdd-contract says each bullet under Guarantees / invariants opens G{n}:. Number them in this touch?

options.label: number them G1 to G9 in their order
options.consequence: The seven existing guarantees keep their text and order and gain ids, with the restart and sign-out guarantees placed after the token guarantee. PRD v2's restart and sign-in tests, and booking-api@v1, can cite one guarantee by id. Nothing cites an auth-api guarantee by id today, so no reference breaks.

options.label: leave them unnumbered
options.consequence: The smallest diff, and the same form as profile-api@v1 and @v2. The new restart and sign-out guarantees are cited by quotation, and the skill's format rule stays unmet on a section this step rewrites anyway.

chosen: number them G1 to G9 in their order
why: The skill's format rule asks for ids so fixtures and phase gates can cite one guarantee, and this run is about to plan backend, web and integration phases (H14 to H19) whose gates name the restart and the token's lifetime. A search of the specs, verification docs and code finds no citation of an auth-api guarantee by id or position, so numbering moves nothing. Ids are prefixes only: no guarantee's text, order or meaning changes, so it is editorial and v1 stays. Existing citations of an auth-api guarantee by number would have argued for leaving them alone.

question: Classify each change of this touch against auth-api@v1's Versioning: G2 naming booking-api@v1, G3 (a restart), G4 (sign-out), the ids G1 to G9, and consumers gaining web.3 and web.4.

options.consequence: No new file, schema or fixtures; status stays stable and phase_ids final. One 2026-10-31 entry under Versioning names each change and why it is compatible. No consumer needs a migration phase, and no ADR affects handoff is due.

options.label: breaking: draft auth-api@v2
options.consequence: A new auth-api.v2.md with its own schema and fixtures identical in shape to v1's, a migration note naming coexisting or lockstep, a breaking-amend stop for a stable versioned contract, and a migration phase or a coexistence window for every consumer, for a change no request or response shows.

chosen: all compatible: v1 stays, one dated Versioning entry
why: auth-api@v1's Versioning names no Breaking line, so the test is the skill's own, 'if a consumer's code could break, it is a new version', read with the contract's earlier entries. G2 naming booking-api@v1 adds a promise and takes none away, the same class as the 2026-10-30 entry that named profile-api@v2 (booking-api@v1 G16 and G17 already rest on it; Q-016). G3 and G4 restate what ADR-001 and RFC-001 §3 have said since v1 and the shipped service does (DEC-057, DEC-058), like the 2026-10-30 code-point clarification. The ids are prefixes (DEC-059) and the consumers are metadata (DEC-056). No endpoint, field, status, code, message, schema or fixture changes; the five fixtures and the schema stay byte for byte. A change any request or response could show, or a consumer that relied on a token outliving a restart, would have made it breaking and a stop.

question: S06's report lists reads outside its inputs (the backend's session code, the web's App test, verification docs, the execution plan and the run's records). Keep the output or rework?

options.consequence: The auth-api touch stands; G3 and G4 are grounded in the shipped code and the verification docs that observed the restart.
